sysd-q-077.title: Double-entry bookkeeping: every debit has a credit
sysd-q-077.text: Every transaction in a company's books is written down twice. In double-entry bookkeeping, each one is recorded with equal and opposite entries: a debit in one ledger account and a credit in a second. Total debits then equal total credits, which is a partial check that the transaction was recorded correctly. The method rests on the accounting equation, and every recorded transaction keeps that equation in balance. A debit is a transfer of value to an account and a credit a transfer from it. A debit increases an asset, while a credit increases a liability. The purpose is accurate financial records in which errors or fraud can be detected. Daybooks, or journals, hold preliminary records that are totalled before posting to the nominal ledger, the main book of accounts. As volume grows, companies use accounting information systems to automate the tracking.

sysd-q-081.title: How money settles: batches, real time and instant
sysd-q-081.text: Settling a payment can take seconds, or it can wait for a batch. A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value. An automated clearing house processes batches as a net settlement system, so settlement may be delayed, which poses settlement risk; it suits low-value, non-urgent transactions. Real-time gross settlement settles each transaction as soon as it is processed, one to one without netting. Its payments are final and irrevocable, and it suits high-value, urgent ones. Instant payment systems run 24x7x365 and complete a transfer, from debit of the payer's account to credit of the beneficiary's, within 10–15 seconds.

sysd-q-078.title: Payment service providers: accepting cards without a bank deal
sysd-q-078.text: A merchant that wants to accept different payment methods does not have to partner with one bank. A payment service provider, or PSP, makes that possible. This third-party company lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments. It is an intermediary between the consumers who pay and the retailers who accept payment. It sets up the technical connections with acquiring banks, the merchants' banks, and with card networks, and it manages processing and those outside relationships. It often also acts as a gateway, the subject of {{ref:sysd-q-079}}. Beyond processing, a PSP may offer risk management, digital wallets, reporting, currency exchange and fraud protection. Fees are typically a percentage of each transaction or a fixed cost per transaction. The merchant remains responsible for data protection, so compliance with PCI DSS matters. A PSP must follow one of four levels set by annual transaction volume, from Level 1 over 6 million to Level 4 under 20,000.

sysd-q-079.title: Payment gateways: carrying payment details, never the money
sysd-q-079.text: A payment gateway sits in the middle of a card payment, yet it is not directly involved in the money flow. It is a merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores. Typically it is a web server to which the merchant's website or point of sale system is connected. It passes payment information between a payment portal, such as a website or mobile phone, and the front end processor or acquiring bank. One gateway often connects several acquiring banks and payment methods under one system. Some let transaction data go straight from the customer's browser to the gateway, bypassing the merchant's systems, using a redirect or an iframe. Many also screen orders for fraud before the authorization request goes to the processor. A bank or a specialised provider such as a PSP can supply one. White label gateways let PSPs, e-commerce platforms or acquiring banks brand the technology as their own.

sysd-q-080.title: Approved in seconds, funded in days: a card payment
sysd-q-080.text:
A card payment is approved in about 2–3 seconds, yet from authorization to funding it typically takes 2-3 days. The two stages are separate, and each has its own trip through the banks.

First comes authorization. The merchant forwards the transaction details to the gateway. The gateway converts the message from XML to ISO 8583 or a variant and passes it to the processor used by the merchant's acquiring bank. The processor forwards the details to the card association, such as Visa or Mastercard. The association may act as the issuing bank or route the transaction to the correct card issuing bank. The issuing bank approves or denies with a response code and a failure reason. The answer returns through the processor and gateway to the website, typically in 2–3 seconds, and the issuer holds an authorization for the approved amount.

Then comes clearing and settlement. After the merchant fulfills the order, the process repeats to clear the authorization. That moves the issuing bank's auth-hold to a debit and prepares settlement with the acquiring bank. At the end of the day the merchant submits its approved authorizations as a batch to its acquiring bank via its processor. The acquiring bank then makes a batch settlement request of the card issuer. The issuer pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day, and the acquiring bank deposits the approved funds into the merchant's account the same or next day.

sysd-q-008.title: Payment reconciliation: the safety net behind exactly-once
sysd-q-008.text:
Even a payment system that charges each customer exactly once still needs a second system to check its work. That system performs reconciliation: comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other. It is always necessary, even with the exactly-once semantics of {{ref:sysd-reliab-070}}, because there are many places that can go wrong. It is a safety net.

Take a $200 PayPal purchase. Under double-entry bookkeeping it appears in three places. The e-commerce site holds a $200 order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller. Reconciliation lines these records up. Formats are the first obstacle: one system writes the timestamp "2022/01/01" and another "Jan 1, 2022", so a layer transforms them into the same format. Volume is the second, and big data processing handles it. A streaming platform such as Flink serves near real-time reconciliation, as in {{ref:sysd-msg-043}}. End-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop is the other route, as in {{ref:sysd-msg-133}}.

Timing is the third. Say the daily cut-off is 00:00:00. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy. Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records. If a match is found, the break is cleared and no more action is needed.

sysd-q-007.title: Designing a payment system that charges exactly once
sysd-q-007.text:
The question is how to design the system that takes a customer's payment for an order and moves the money correctly. One requirement comes before all others. The system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems it can have.

The flow starts when a user clicks the Buy button. A payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores it in the database. One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout. The payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order. The executor stores the order, then calls an external payment service provider, or PSP, to finish the credit card payment. A PSP is a third-party intermediary with connections to acquiring banks and card networks. The card payment goes through the processor and card association to the issuing bank, which approves or denies with a response code. The round trip typically takes 2–3 seconds.

Once the payment succeeds, the payment service updates the wallet with how much the seller holds. It then calls the ledger service, which appends the new ledger information to the database. The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping, explained in {{ref:sysd-q-077}}: each transaction is recorded as equal and opposite debit and credit entries, so debits equal credits. This keeps records accurate and lets errors or fraud be detected. Take a $200 watch paid through PayPal. The site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.

Exactly-once, the guarantee in {{ref:sysd-reliab-070}}, becomes easier when split in two. At-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check. When the PSP call fails on a network error or timeout, the client retries the payment, which may succeed at a later attempt. The idempotency key, covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-073}}, stops the retry from charging twice. It is usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, and it goes in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key. Checking and recording the key must be atomic, so that no other request can slip in between, for example with a unique constraint or Redis SET NX.

Afterward the system checks itself. Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files holding the bank account balance and the day's transactions; for cards, authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days. Reconciliation, described in {{ref:sysd-q-008}}, compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match. A layer transforms different formats into one, and big data processing handles volume: Flink for near real-time, or end-of-day batch such as Hadoop. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off. It is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches. Reconciliation is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.

One duty sits outside the flow of money. The PSP must follow PCI DSS at one of four compliance levels set by annual transaction volume, and gateways screen orders for fraud before authorization. To remember: retry freely, charge once, record both sides of every transaction, and check again afterward.

openers.design-a-payment-system: Double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems a payment system can have, so it must execute each payment order exactly once. This chapter builds toward that demand from the ground up. It starts with the bookkeeping method that keeps the books balanced and with the systems that settle financial transactions by transferring monetary value. It then follows a card payment through the third-party companies, the payment service provider and the gateway, that let businesses accept electronic payments. It ends with the process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match, and with a full design that ties it all together.

reviews.design-a-payment-system: Every payment is recorded twice, as a debit and a credit, so the books balance. Settlement systems differ in speed, from batches through real-time gross settlement to instant transfers, and a card payment is approved in 2–3 seconds but funded 2-3 days later. The payment service provider and the gateway sit between merchant and bank, with the gateway never touching the money flow. Because many places can go wrong, even a system with exactly-once semantics needs reconciliation as a safety net, and the full design uses an idempotency key so that a retry cannot charge twice.
